agent: Claude Code (CLAUDE.md, this repository) — fix: decide() accepted any person's verdict with no permission check at all
summary_for_principal: A third permission gap, found the same way as the first two — by checking, not assuming, before actually running the worked example. This one is the most direct: the call that records a person's final approve/deny decision on a gate had no authorization check whatsoever. Any caller, holding no permission at all, could decide any gate any way they liked, and the engine would accept it and act on it. Fixed to check the same permission the gate declares for that decision — the specific reviewer's permission if one is named, or the gate's own fallback permission otherwise, matching the rulebook's own two documented cases. A person whose gate declares a role instead of a permission string is refused outright, since the engine has no way to check a role — flagged rather than guessed at. Four new tests, covering the refusal, the denial, and both of the two documented permission sources. Full suite: 306 tests pass. This closes the last of the permission-checking gaps this evaluation set out looking for; every action the engine can take — running a step, an agent voting on an approval, a person deciding one — now goes through the same check before anything happens.

also.reason: Four new tests: no permission declared, permission denied, and the two D13-documented permission sources (a named decider's own permission; the gate's own fallback permission when no decider is at that slot).

S389/S391 (person decider shape; D13's gate-permission fallback) and S472 ("...or accepts any decision, it asks the host's PolicyPort") read directly to ground exactly which permission to check in which case, rather than guessing.

interpretation.read_as: Same as the three immediately prior fixes in this evaluation — a verified, in-scope permission-first gap, closed and tested without needing to ask first.

filled_in.gap: A person decider MAY be declared with `role` instead of `permission` (S389: `person: { permission: <host permission> } or { role: <host role> }`), but `PolicyPort.authorize()` only ever takes a permission string — there is no method anywhere in this codebase's ports to check a role.
filled_in.assumed: Refused outright (FORBIDDEN) rather than inventing a role-to-permission mapping or silently accepting an unchecked decision. This is a genuine spec/port gap, not a judgment call I should paper over in code.
filled_in.grounded_in: CLAUDE.md: "If the spec is silent or wrong, do not invent a rule in code: write the gap as a proposed spec change in your PR and flag it in the run record." PolicyPort's own contract (domain/ports/policy.py) has no role-checking method to extend even if I wanted to guess at one.
filled_in.reversal_cost: Cheap — if a future PolicyPort gains a role-checking method (or the format's own vocabulary is amended to route role through permission somehow), this one refusal becomes a real check; nothing else in this fix depends on the guess being right.

decisions.headline: decide() checks the specific person-decider's own `permission` when satisfying a declared decider at its rightful sequence slot, and the GATE's own `permission` (D13's fallback) in every other case — no deciders declared, or every declared decider already exhausted (the pause state).
decisions.problem: Unlike the STEP and GATE-agent-decider fixes (a single Tool's own permission), a GATE can be decided by a person for two structurally different reasons the spec itself distinguishes (S391): satisfying one specific declared `person`-kind decider (checked against that decider's own permission), or the D13 fallback where the gate's own permission stands in (no deciders at all, or the pause after every declared decider answers INDETERMINATE).
options_rejected: Always check only the GATE's own permission, ignoring any per-decider permission: rejected — contradicts S389/S391's own text, which gives a person decider its own `permission`/`role` distinct from the gate's; a host that wants different reviewers authorized differently for the same gate (e.g. a `person` decider one role can satisfy, vs. a supervisor-only fallback) would have no way to express that.

Reconstruct the gate's true current resolution via resolve_gate (needing run_state, like the agent-decider fix) rather than the simpler decider_index/len(node.deciders) check used here: rejected for this pass — decide() never needed run_state before (no evidence/separation-of-duty check applies to a person's decision, S7.6 reserves that for agent deciders only), and the simpler check is sufficient to answer the one question decide() actually needs answered (which permission gates this specific call), without importing the heavier machinery `_report_gate_decision` needed for a genuinely different reason (evidence-path resolution).
decisions.cost_to_change: Localized entirely to decide()'s own new permission-selection logic; no change to _advance_gate, _drive, or any other call path.

evidence.claim: Before this fix, decide() recorded any verdict from any caller with zero calls to ctx.policy.authorize() anywhere in the function — confirmed by reading the function directly before making any change.
evidence.source: src/sulis_workflows/engine/run.py, decide(), read directly this session before the fix.

evidence.claim: Both of D13's documented permission sources are now correctly selected and checked: a declared person decider's own permission when satisfying it at its slot; the gate's own permission when no decider occupies that slot (the `deciders=()` case tested directly).

decisions.revisit_if: A future work package adds a way to check a person's `role` (a new PolicyPort method, or a format decision that role resolves through permission somehow) — the FORBIDDEN-outright treatment for `role` should be revisited then, not before.

flags.subject: docs/spec/process-definition.md S389 (`person: { role: <host role> }`) vs. src/sulis_workflows/domain/ports/policy.py (PolicyPort.authorize() takes only a permission string)
flags.tension: The format's own text allows a person decider to be declared by `role` as an alternative to `permission`, but the engine's only authorization primitive (PolicyPort.authorize()) has no way to check a role — there is no method, and ADR-024 only defines permission strings as the host's grammar, saying nothing about roles.
standards_in_play: sulis-ai/platform ADR-024 (permission strings are the host's grammar)
flags.need: A decision on whether `role` is meant to resolve to a permission string somehow (and if so, how — a host-side lookup this engine would need a new port method to call), or whether `role` should be removed from the format's own vocabulary as unimplementable with the current port shape.

options.option: Add a `PolicyPort.authorize_role()` (or similar) method and route `person: {role: ...}` through it.
options.consequence: A genuinely new port method, a real design task (what does a role check even return — the same PERMIT/DENY/INDETERMINATE?), and every existing PolicyPort adapter would need updating.

options.option: Remove `role` from the format's own vocabulary, keeping only `permission` for person deciders.
options.consequence: A spec change (small); any real process definition already written against the spec's `role` form (none exist yet outside this repository) would need rewriting.

options.option: Leave it exactly as this fix does — refused outright — indefinitely.
options.consequence: A person decider declared with `role` can never actually be decided by anyone, ever, on any process; effectively dead syntax that validates but can never run.

flags.recommendation: Given no real process definition uses `role` yet and no fixture in this repository ever has, the third option (leave it refused) is the safest default until you decide there is real demand for role-based person deciders — but it should not stay silently undecided forever, since a process author who writes `role` today gets a definition that validates but can never be decided.
flags.safe_default: Refuse (current behaviour) — cheaper to widen later than to have silently accepted unchecked decisions in the meantime.

lessons.maxim: "Permission first" (CLAUDE.md's own principle) needs to be checked as a property of every distinct ACTION the engine can be asked to take, not assumed true because it was proven true for one of them — three separate call sites (STEP dispatch, GATE agent vote, GATE person decision) each independently lacked the check, found one at a time, each only by trying to actually complete the corresponding action rather than by re-reading the principle and assuming it already held everywhere.
lessons.incident: This is the third of three permission-first gaps found in this one evaluation session, each in a structurally different part of the engine (STEP's TOOL_STEP hand-off, GATE's agent-decider completion, GATE's decide()) and each found only by trying to drive each action to completion, not by any kind of review that assumed the principle held because it held elsewhere.
lessons.destination: Any future audit of this engine's own conformance to CLAUDE.md's "permission first": check next()/report()/decide()/skip() as four SEPARATE surfaces, each on its own, rather than trusting that one being correct means the others are.
lessons.proposed_check: The three permission-gap run records from this session (STEP: docs/runs/01M2SY9THTDDHTDFQRK6RYZCWE; GATE agent: docs/runs/01M2SZYTXVTK6V2FKRWJN6N2VE; GATE person: this record) are themselves the check — three of this engine's four action-taking calls needed the same fix independently.
